newsitem.title: USA: Maine House rejects June vote on forestry proposal.
newsitem.headline: Maine House rejects June vote on forestry proposal.

text.p: The Maine House of Representatives on Thursday rejected a bill that would have scheduled a June referendum on a measure to overhaul the state's logging rules.
The referendum is required as a follow-up to a ballot question last November in which voters chose among three competing proposals on a practice known as clear cutting.

The proposal that won the most support was a compromise position put forward last summer by the administration of Gov. Angus King, the forest products industry and a group of environmental organizations. It would tighten restrictions on clear cutting and other logging rules but would not impose an outright ban on the practice.
In the next referedum, voters will be asked to ratify that proposal or reject it.
Supporters of a special election in June said the time had come to settle the dispute. Opponents said there was no need to rush the issue and holding a June vote would cost too much.
The House on Thursday left open debate on setting a date for the vote. Gov. Angus King favors a referendum in November, when other local elections are held.

"Are we some sort banana republic where elections can be put off to meet the needs of some party's agenda? We're Maine, not Ecuador." said Rep. William Lemke. He said delaying the vote until after June could give opponents of the proposal time to mount a stronger challenge.

The proposal was put on the ballot last year as an alternative to a measure drafted by leaders of Maine's Green Party that would have banned clear cutting in Maine's North Woods. The third measure on the 1996 ballot would have left current rules unchanged.
